ta-l1d39q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 39. Lombard asks what kind of cause divine knowledge is: whether it is invariable, and whether it is universal (against an apparent objection from Jerome). On invariability, he determines that God's knowledge is wholly immutable, granting locutions that imply variation on the side of the things known but not of the knowledge, denying what must simply be denied, and reporting the opinion of some who grant locutions like 'God can know more than he knows', referring them to variety in the known. On universality he answers Jerome's objection and recapitulates that God knows all things simultaneously and immutably. Thomas asks two questions, on the invariability of God's knowledge and on the universality of his providence. On the first, three articles: whether God can not know what he knows; whether he can know something he does not know, or more than he knows; and whether God knows infinitely many things.
claims: God's knowledge is wholly immutable; variation is on the side of the known.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e128.summary: First argument that God cannot not know what he knows. God cannot make the past not to have been (Augustine, Jerome, the Philosopher), and 'this is known by God' is signified as past.
claims: God cannot change the past.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e131.summary: Second argument, rejecting the reply that it is a past depending on the future, since the participle implies not only an order to the future but an act (as said earlier; the cross-reference reads Dist. 37, apparently meaning the discussion in Dist. 38).
claims: 'Known' implies an act, not just future reference.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e134.summary: Third argument. Whatever is, necessarily is while it is (the Philosopher), and God's knowing is always in act, measured by eternity, so it cannot not be.
claims: What is, necessarily is while it is.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e138.summary: Fourth argument. Everything eternal is necessary (the Philosopher), and every knowing of God is eternal.
claims: The eternal is necessary.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e141.summary: Fifth argument. His knowing is his being, and he cannot not be.
claims: God's knowing is his being.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e144.summary: Sed contra. Whatever God knows operatively he works, and he can not work what he works, so he can not know what he knows.
claims: God can refrain from working.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e147.summary: Thomas's determination. As the divine attributes differ in concept though one thing, their acts follow their concepts, so something is attributed to one act and not another: God knows what he does not will or do. It belongs to will to produce its act freely (Augustine: what is done by will is not done by necessity), so it can will and not will, but only while the act is going out from the will; once passed, it is not in its power, since it cannot not have willed what it willed; nor can it produce both at once. This holds for acts commanded by the will too, like thinking and speaking. Since the act of the divine will is always in act and never passes into the past, it is always as it were going out from the will, so the will keeps its freedom toward it: God can not will this, but cannot will and not will at once, or will now and not later, 'now' and 'later' taken on the side of the will, which cannot change. Since the act of divine knowledge, as cause of his work by informing it, is commanded by the will (Dist. 8), God can in this way not foreknow, but cannot foreknow and not foreknow at once, or foreknow now and not later, speaking of foreknowledge on the side of knowledge only, disregarding the character of future, since what is future becomes present and is then known, not foreknown. So, with Lombard's distinction, taken conjointly (in the composite sense) God cannot not know what he knows; taken divisively it is in his power to know and not know, which expresses his freedom.
claims: God's operative knowledge, commanded by his eternal will, remains free: in the divided sense he can not know what he knows.
In the composite sense he cannot not know what he knows, since his will cannot change.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the first argument. The act of divine knowledge never passes into the past but is always in act, so it remains in the freedom of the will.
claims: Divine knowing is never past.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the second argument: that solution is worthless.
claims: The 'past dependent on future' reply fails.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e157.summary: Reply to the third argument. What is necessarily is while it is, but not absolutely; likewise God necessarily knows while he knows, but not necessarily except by necessity of immobility, which does not exclude freedom of will, expressed when we say God can not know or not will this.
claims: Necessity of immobility is compatible with freedom.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e160.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Everything eternal is necessary by necessity of immobility, which does not exclude freedom of will (Dist. 8).
claims: Eternal necessity is necessity of immobility.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e163.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Though being and knowing are really the same, knowing follows the will as commanded by it and being does not, so his being is not subject to the freedom of his will as his operative knowledge of creatures is.
claims: Operative knowing, unlike being, is subject to will.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e175.summary: First argument that God cannot know what he does not know. God knows existing things only through ideas, and no idea can be in him that is not, since a form cannot come to God without his change.
claims: New ideas would change God.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e178.summary: Second argument. Knowledge is really related to and depends on the knowable, and what depends changes when its term changes, so if something could be known by God that is not now, his knowledge could change.
claims: Knowledge depends on the knowable.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e181.summary: Third argument. The quantity of knowledge follows the quantity of knowables, so if he could know something he does not, he could know more and his knowledge could increase, which is impossible.
claims: More knowables, more knowledge.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e185.summary: Fourth argument. God knows not only what is but what is not (Dist. 38), and there is nothing besides being and non-being, so he cannot know anything besides what he knows.
claims: Nothing lies between being and non-being.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e188.summary: Sed contra. God can work what he does not work, and he works whatever he works by his knowledge, so he can know something besides what he knows.
claims: God can work otherwise.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e191.summary: Thomas's determination. God knows by knowledge of vision, seeing what is, will be, or was not only in their causes' potency but in their own being, or by knowledge of simple understanding, knowing what never exists as in their causes' potency. By the latter God cannot know anything besides what he knows, since nothing can be besides what is and what can be. By knowledge of vision, which Lombard speaks of, he can see something besides what he sees, since he can give being in its own nature to what is only in his power, though if he did, it would have been foreknown from eternity. So the same distinction applies: conjointly, God cannot know what he does not know, since 'God knows what he did not know from eternity' is incompossible; divisively it is true, expressing the power of freedom, not mutability of knowledge or will.
claims: By simple understanding God knows all possibles and can know nothing more.
By vision, in the divided sense, he can know what he does not, since he could make it exist.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e194.summary: Reply to the first argument. An idea is one in essence and distinguished only by respects, so another thing would add a respect, not a form. Or better, as knowing itself is subject to the freedom of the will, so is the idea, as the act of divine knowledge terminates in it, as an artisan's knowledge in the form of the artefact he devises; as one cannot posit that the act of knowing is in him and was not, neither that an idea is in him and was not, yet freedom of will applies to both.
claims: Ideas, like knowing, are subject to divine freedom without change.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e197.summary: Reply to the second argument. Our knowledge depends on the knowable, but the knowable depends on God's knowledge, so as our knowledge varies while the knowable stays, the knowable changes while God's knowledge does not.
claims: Things depend on God's knowledge, not conversely.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e200.summary: Reply to the third argument. Though in some way it is granted that God can know something besides what he knows, it does not seem grantable that he can know more than he knows, since 'more' implies comparison with something pre-existing without which this was, and 'he did not know before and knows now' cannot both be true, nor can God bring it about; so 'he can know more' pertains somewhat to the composite sense, and Lombard only reports this opinion, and likewise nothing should be said to be added to his knowledge. Even if granted, his knowledge could not increase, since he knows many and few by one and the same primary object, his essence, its likeness.
claims: 'God can know more than he knows' should not be granted; his knowledge cannot increase.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e204.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God does not know what is not by knowledge of vision, and only that is in question here.
claims: The question concerns knowledge of vision.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e216.summary: First argument that God knows infinitely many things. Knowledge is numbered by the known, and Ps. 146:5 says of his wisdom there is no number.
claims: His wisdom has no number.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e222.summary: Second argument. God knows all species of number alike, and he knows determinately whatever species any man knows, and the species of numbers are infinite.
claims: Species of numbers are infinite.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e225.summary: Third argument. Particulars are infinite, and God knows particulars (Dist. 36).
claims: Particulars are infinite.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e229.summary: Fourth argument. God's power is called infinite and of infinitely many things simply, and he can make nothing except by knowledge, so his knowledge is simply of infinitely many.
claims: Infinite power implies infinite knowledge.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e232.summary: First contrary argument. Whatever is known is perfectly comprehended, and what is comprehended is bounded by the intellect's comprehension (Augustine; Metaphysics 2), and the infinite cannot be bounded.
claims: Comprehension bounds its object.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e235.summary: Second contrary argument, against 'infinite in itself, finite relative to God'. What is said of something differently relative to different things is relational, as great and small; being infinite is absolute, so what is infinite in itself is finite relative to nothing.
claims: Infinity is absolute.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e238.summary: Third contrary argument. The infinite is infinite to the finite because it cannot be traversed, and it cannot be traversed by the infinite either (Physics 4).
claims: The infinite cannot be traversed.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e241.summary: Fourth contrary argument. Whatever is known in act is in the knower in act, and infinitely many things cannot be in act.
claims: No actual infinite.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e244.summary: Thomas's determination. The infinite is taken in two ways. Intensively, as continuous quantity, God does not know an infinite in act, since infinite continuous quantity neither is nor can be, unless he is said to know the infinite in knowing himself, who is infinite. As discrete quantity, God by knowledge of simple understanding knows infinitely many things in his power, not only individuals but species, since he could create infinitely many other species and knows he can. By knowledge of vision, seeing things in their own being, his knowledge is not of infinitely many, not from any defect of his knowledge but of things, which are not infinite numbered over all time; if the world had always been and would never end, as philosophers held, his knowledge of vision would be of infinitely many. This cannot fit our knowledge, which knows singulars properly only through different forms taken from them and so understands one after another (Dist. 35), so to understand infinitely many would be to number infinitely many, which is impossible; yet our intellect understands infinitely many in a way, understanding a universal form potential to infinitely many singulars, which is why philosophers prove the intellect immaterial, having a kind of infinite power, impossible for a power in matter. The divine intellect understands all that is or can be by one thing, its essence, not only universally but properly and determinately (Dist. 35), so it does not know different things by any transition but sees all at one glance, and so nothing prevents its being of infinitely many.
claims: By simple understanding God knows infinitely many possibles; by vision only as many as exist over time.
God's one non-discursive glance can embrace infinitely many, which our successive intellect cannot.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e248.summary: Reply to the first argument. God's knowledge is said to have no number because of its infinite power of comprehending, not because of an infinity of things known by determinate knowledge of vision.
claims: 'No number' refers to comprehending power.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e251.summary: Reply to the second argument. God knows some species of numbers by knowledge of vision, not all, since given a beginning and end of the world there is some number that things existing in time do not exceed; but he knows all by simple understanding.
claims: All numbers are known by simple understanding.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e254.summary: Reply to the third argument. The number of particulars is infinite simply only if the world is eternal, which is against faith.
claims: Particulars are finite given a non-eternal world.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e257.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Power regards as object possible being, whose concept does not depend on actual being, so even if infinitely many are never actualized over time, power is called simply of infinitely many. Knowledge's object is the true, convertible with being, so it is not called simply of what never has actual being, but only in some respect, as they are said to be in a cause's potency in some respect.
claims: Power is of possibles simply; knowledge of non-actuals only in some respect.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the first contrary argument. An intellect running through a thing cannot comprehend an infinite thing, since it would bound it by numbering its parts, but God's knowledge without discursus is uniformly of one and many, finite and infinite.
claims: Non-discursive knowledge comprehends without numbering.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e263.summary: The second contrary argument is granted.
claims: The infinite is not finite relative to anything.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e267.summary: Reply to the third contrary argument. The divine intellect does not understand by traversing, so the objection fails.
claims: God does not traverse.

ta-l1d39q1-d1e270.summary: Reply to the fourth contrary argument. Everything God knows is one in him, distinguished only by different respects, and it is not unfitting that relations following the intellect's operation be infinite (Avicenna).
claims: Infinitely many relations of reason are possible.

ta-l1d39q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 39 divides Lombard's treatment of the invariability and universality of divine knowledge and announces two questions, the first with three articles on whether God can not know what he knows, whether he can know more, and whether he knows infinitely many things.
claims: God's knowledge is immutable.

ta-l1d39q1-Dd1e120.summary: Article 1 holds that God's operative knowledge, commanded by his eternal will, remains free. In the divided sense he can not know what he knows; in the composite sense he cannot, since his will cannot change. His knowing is never past, and the necessity of immobility of eternal acts does not exclude freedom.
claims: God can not know what he knows in the divided, not the composite, sense.

ta-l1d39q1-Dd1e167.summary: Article 2 holds that by simple understanding God knows all possibles and can know nothing more, while by vision, in the divided sense, he can know what he does not, since he could make it exist. Things depend on his knowledge, not conversely. 'He can know more than he knows' should not be granted, and his knowledge cannot increase.
claims: God can know otherwise only in the divided sense and by vision.

ta-l1d39q1-Dd1e208.summary: Article 3 holds that God knows infinitely many possibles, species as well as individuals, by simple understanding, and by vision only as many as exist over time, which would be infinite only if the world were eternal. His one non-discursive glance can embrace infinitely many, which our successive intellect cannot, though our intellect's grasp of universals shows its immateriality.
claims: God knows infinitely many by simple understanding, through one non-discursive glance.

ta-l1d39q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 39 treats the invariability of God's knowledge. Article 1 holds that God's operative knowledge, commanded by his eternal will, is free: in the divided sense he can not know what he knows, though not in the composite sense. Article 2 holds that by vision, in the divided sense, he can know what he does not, while his knowledge of possibles is complete and cannot increase. Article 3 holds that he knows infinitely many possibles by simple understanding in one glance.
claims: God's knowledge is immutable yet free in the divided sense.
God knows infinitely many possibles by one glance.
